title: Trump claims revised economic data shows pre-midterms figures were ‘fake’ | First Thing
summary: President calls for investigation after GDP figures were adjusted upwards, despite revisions to official economic figures being commonplace. Plus, the weird and macabre world of Victorian…

blocks.text: Good morning. Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.

In a holiday message on his Truth Social platform, the US president wished a happy Thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

items: Why did Trump call the figures fake? Revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, but Trump has tried repeatedly to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is under way in the US. “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.

What other acerbic well-wishes did Trump offer? He wished “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.

blocks.text: Georgia judge blocks own order to turn over US election ballot copies to state board

blocks.caption: The judge paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal. Photograph: Mike Stewart/AP

blocks.text: A judge in Fulton county, Georgia, has blocked her own order to turn over electronic copies of 2020 election ballots seized by the FBI in a raid to the state election board. Superior court judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

items: Why are the ballots at the center of an ongoing dispute over the 2020 election? Some Republicans, led by Trump, claimed the election results had been rigged despite Joe Biden being certified after several recounts. Republican state officials had refused to overturn the result, despite a now-infamous phone call from Trump to pressure the Georgia secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, to “find 11,780 votes”.

blocks.text: US Senate ‘permitting bill’ threatens clean water protections to speed up energy projects

blocks.caption: The law would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, advocates warn. Photograph: Gerry Broome/AP

blocks.text: An industry-backed “permitting bill” approved by the US Senate would gut key clean water protections with changes that would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, politicians are being warned.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and datacenters.
‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

blocks.caption: Paramedics assist an activist who was attacked by Israeli settlers during the olive harvest season. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Since 7 October 2023, Israeli soldiers and militant settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian paramedics and blocked them from reaching the wounded in the West Bank. Violence against healthcare workers rose by more than 350% between 2022 and 2024, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel, a non-profit organisation which documents human rights abuse affecting the right to health in the occupied Palestinian territory.
In other news …

blocks.caption: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on goods from China. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

items: Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.
A 44-year-old man who was trying to help his son navigate an icy patch fell to his death on a southern California mountain trail.

The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives. Faced with criticism of the potentially hazardous detonation the Trump administration made a concerted effort to blame former president Barack Obama.

Thousands of girls and women have reported bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas. Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October have given testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles.
Final election results in New Zealand show the ruling coalition needs minor party support to govern.

blocks.text: Stat of the day: More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thanksgiving evening

blocks.caption: Heavy rain and strong winds in New Jersey on Thanksgiving. Photograph: Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Storms flooded communities in the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. Macy’s Thanksgiving parade in New York was postponed for the first time.
Culture Pick: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas

blocks.caption: Maddie Ziegler and Graham Phillips in In a Holidaze. Photograph: Bettina Strauss/Netflix © 2026

blocks.text: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Louis Staples speaks to stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid, who explain why the format is so hard to resist.
Don’t miss this: Killer frogs and rat-murdering fairies – the macabre cards British Victorians sent at Christmas

blocks.caption: Fairies roasting their dinner. Photograph: Mary Evans Picture Library/The David Pearson Collection

blocks.text: Continuing the Christmas theme, Esther Addley looks at the history of the Christmas card, and discovers the “absurd and unexpectedly violent” images that give a glimpse into the darker, more subversive side of 19th-century festivities.
… or this: ‘These families will be essentially homeless’ – Flatbush groups condemn response to building collapse

blocks.caption: People observe a moment of silence during a rally against negligence by landlords. Photograph: Adam Gray/Getty Images

blocks.text: Flatbush community leaders are in an uproar on behalf of those who have been displaced in the aftermath of an apartment building collapse in Brooklyn earlier this month, saying that families were sent to “subpar hotels” infested with roaches and mice until 30 November, with no housing plans in place afterward. This feature by Auzzy Byrdsell explains the tumult taking hold of a New York City community.
Climate check: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record

blocks.caption: Lake Titicaca shrinks amid extreme drought. Photograph: Claudia Morales/Reuters

blocks.text: Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.
Last Thing: Amanda Seyfried needed ‘five-factor authentication’ to read You Can See Everything script – but still ‘told everyone’ anyway

blocks.caption: Amanda Seyfried: ‘I’m the most indiscreet person I’ve ever met.’ Photograph: Bruce Glikas/Getty Images

blocks.text: Amanda Seyfried, who had previously played the convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the TV drama The Dropout, has revealed how she was drafted in to the hit documentary You Can See Everything “at the last minute” – but said she found it difficult keeping her involvement in the film secret for over a year. “I’m the most indiscreet person I’ve ever met in my life,” she said.
